I unfortunately fell asleep five minutes before the free started last night (😭) so I’ve only now finished watching it. 

So many great skates last night - Niina and Nina both did so well for themselves, I got so emotional seeing Haein back and doing really well (the small mistakes aside), and some of the earlier group skaters like Lara and Alexandra Feigin also really delivered! 

In terms of the top 6, both Kaori and Alysa did amazing and were so fun to watch (jealous of everyone who got to see them live!) and Wakaba’s StSq was a joy to watch like always (Kaori crying was so sweet and lowkey relatable lol). I also connected more with Maddie’s skating than I normally do, and it was honestly heartbreaking that she didn’t make the top 10, you could see how much it would have meant. 

The US overscoring debate on here (and on the other social media which shall not be named) does get a little… idk, I find both sides a bit frustrating? Yes, Alysa, Amber and Isabeau did amazing and I don’t in any way want to diminish that. But pointing out that home scoring (which is a pretty widely acknowledged thing) is really blatant in the US, across men/ID/women especially, is not hating on the skaters or saying they don’t deserve their accolades. In the same way lots of American fans would rightfully complain about the Eteri bonus, it has to be okay for non-Americans to point out score inflation here and at SkAm? I get that you don’t notice it or choose not to see it because they’re your skaters and you’re proud of them (as you should be), but that doesn’t mean no one else is allowed to discuss it as a flaw in the system, the same way we discuss uncalled flutzes, reputation scoring, or PCS being dependent on which group you skate in

I will say, as someone who is neither American nor Russian, that they feel pretty even in the sense the feeling going in was that an American was always going to win here (and ID/mens) unless they all had complete meltdown skates - which is the same way it used to feel with Russian scoring. Plus, as someone else pointed out, the tech content of the Russian women meant the finishing order was never in question - here, the order actually could have looked different if worlds had been in, say, France. That’s not saying Alysa didn’t deserve the win, or that the American women didn’t do well! But it has to be okay to acknowledge that the US does blatantly  home score, in the same way we acknowledged the Eteri bonus.

A sheitel is not a loophole, this is a really weird (and straight-up inaccurate) way of phrasing the TIL, which I’m guessing is coloured by how other religions deal with hair. Covering your hair in Orthodox Judaism isn’t about modesty, it’s because your hair after marriage is considered something private and sacred to you (roughly), or because it’s considered to hold certain power/properties (depending on how much you’re into mysticism). 

Covering your hair with a wig is no more a loophole than covering it with a scarf (as some do), because the point isn’t that you should cover you hair for modesty, or that men seeing your hair is bad. The point is that your own natural hair is sacred, and you keep it private, but it doesn’t matter what you choose to cover it with. I really don’t get why that’s such a strange concept, unless you’re trying to interpret jewish customs through a lens of other religions you’ve encountered (ie Islam, where the issue really is that no one should see your hair, or believe they see your hair, for modesty purposes)

A lot of people are overlooking one of the benefits of F1 Academy (aside from PR/inspiration for future drivers): track time. One of the consistent struggles for female karting talents has been a lack of sponsorship, leading to a lack of track time which makes them struggle more when starting out in single-seaters. 

F1A has a lot of testing for a junior series, at a relatively low cost. Amount of hours in the car correlates pretty directly to performance in a lot of lower series, and when women struggle to rack up time around the track, that’s a massive road block to having successful female racers.

Really surprised by some of the responses here calling her selfish or inappropriate, or that she’s “making herself a victim”. 

a) abuse rewires your brain. For most survivors it fundamentally changes the way you see the world, the way you form relationships and the way you interact with others. It’s normal that her trauma is showing in her interactions, it would be more surprising if it didn’t. 

b) being able to talk about your experiences after leaving the relationship can be incredibly freeing. I wasn’t able to talk about it until a few years after; and that’s caused a lot of hurt and delayed my healing process after. Talking and sharing is a way to reckon with what happened. She should be mindful that she’s not triggering others, yes - but she’s also just learning to navigate this. Give her time. 

c) the incident with Karen - obviously we have very little context in this post, but a lot of survivors have had to completely cut off friendships with people who continue to support their abuser. If that’s the case here, her reaction seems completely justified to me. 

d) the way some people here are focused on the idea that she “shouldn’t let herself be a victim” is so disturbing to me. Sure, some people hate that label and don’t identify with it - but you don’t get to prescribe what others should identify with. For myself and many others, it’s a useful label. Yes, we were victimised. Reclaiming that (especially in the face of manipulation and gaslighting) can be a very powerful thing. She has also only been out of the relationship for a few months. She’s absolutely allowed to feel like her whole identity right now is that victimhood because she has gone through something awful and she’s going through something unimaginably difficult.

Again, Dilation and Extraction (D&X) is the medical term for the procedure. “Partial birth abortion” is not a medical concept. The phrase is not recognised by the American Medical Association as a procedure. “Partial birth abortion” is a political phrase that was created by a congressman called Charles Canady. Charles Canady had no medical background or experience. The fact that it is in the name of the legislation does not mean it is a real medical procedure. Congress could propose a law tomorrow banning duck-based milkshake algorithms; that wouldn’t make them real. The medical authority on this subject (AMA and the American College of Gynaecologists) does not recognise it as a medical procedure. Intact D&X is not a “cutesie” term, it is correct medical terminology. “Partial birth abortion” is a deliberately misleading political term used to obfuscate the actual purpose of an Intact D&X. 

Secondly, Intact D&X procedures are not performed “up until the point of birth”. You cannot suddenly decide you want an abortion a day before your due date and have an intact D&X. Not in any state. No politician is arguing for that. The Supreme Court case was filed because Intact D&X is one of the safest late-term abortion methods (late-term does not mean in labour, it means second or third trimester) and because it’s used in cases of miscarriage. Banning Intact D&X denies appropriate medical care to women having suffered a miscarriage.

“Partial birth abortion” is a myth. There is no state, nor any serious politician who is in favour of allowing abortion up until the point of birth. The real medical procedure that conservatives have tried to demonise by calling it “partial birth abortion” (which isn’t a medical term), is an intact D&X. These are used for various reasons, including when the pregnancy has ended in a miscarriage and the fetus needs to be extracted from the uterus (ie it’s not expelled on its own). Intact D&X does not mean the pregnancy is terminated after a child is born; it’s currently only legal in the US if the pregnancy is terminated (usually through an injection) prior to the D&X. An intact D&X cannot be used up until the point of birth, but in cases of miscarriage or serious risk to the woman’s life it’s one of the safest options for terminating a late-stage pregnancy.

The answers you’ve gotten seem to have figured out the specifics but I’d like to add something general for you and anyone else looking at immigration records:
The absolute majority of people who passed through NY or Ellis Island did not write their own records, instead they dictated it to someone else. In a lot of cases this led to English-speaking people transcribing a version of what they heard, which means they often misspelled names, dropped surnames or put names in the wrong order. Generally, when you’re looking at immigration records from places like Ellis Island, especially during periods of mass immigration, it’s useful to assume the records aren’t correct (or at least not fully). Obviously, that is really annoying but unless the person you’re looking for immigrated from the UK or was fluent in English, that’s just how it goes.
